title: BGP Route Flap Damping
summary: Describes a technique for BGP that reduces routing traffic and router load by penalizing routes that change too often, without hurting convergence for stable routes. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Some destinations in the Internet keep appearing and disappearing from routing tables. Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) routers can use route flap damping to quiet such a destination. Each withdrawal adds a penalty to the route, the penalty fades over time, and a route whose penalty passes a set limit is held back until the penalty has fallen far enough. Stable routes are barely delayed.

how does bgp route flap damping work
subtitle: Route flap damping: a router holds back a route that keeps changing, and lets it through again once it settles.

tldr.problem: Destinations that change reachability too often, called route flap, make every router that hears the change do more work, and an overloaded router can fail and overload its neighbours.
tldr.mechanism: Each router keeps a figure of merit per route, adds 1 to it on every withdrawal and lets it decay exponentially over time. Above the cutoff threshold the route is suppressed and not advertised; below the lower reuse threshold it is advertised again.
tldr.outcome: The mechanism is applied only to routes learned from external BGP peers, never to internal ones, because damping internal routes can create routing loops. The RFC reports deployment experience since 1995 and recommends damping close to the source of the flap.

facts.label: Penalty per withdrawal
facts.value: 1 added to the figure of merit

today: RFC 2439 is a Proposed Standard on the Internet standards track, and no RFC in the site index obsoletes or updates it. The RFC reports more than two years of deployment experience when it was written in 1998, and it describes no later version of the mechanism.

sections.title: Why Route Flap Damping Exists
sections.content:
An excessive rate of change to the advertised reachability of a subset of Internet prefixes has been widespread since the early 1990s. The RFC calls this effect route flap. These updates are not necessarily periodic, so route oscillation would be a misleading name for it.

The processing load comes from two places: the BGP decision process and the adding and removing of forwarding entries. A widely deployed BGP implementation may fail under high routing update volume, for example by being unable to keep its BGP or IGP sessions up. The failure of one router then adds load on other routers, which can cause failures in other instances of the same implementation or of other implementations with a similar weakness. The RFC says such worse cases have already been observed in practice, and that in the worst case a stable oscillation can result.

The mechanism described here contains routing instability at the AS border router that borders the instability, where AS stands for Autonomous System. The RFC is explicit that these guidelines are designed to prevent sustained oscillations, but that they do not eliminate the need for robust and efficient implementations, and that a BGP implementation cannot rely on the sender to shield it from route instabilities.
sections.plainLanguage: Some destinations in the Internet keep appearing and disappearing from routing tables. Each change costs every router that hears about it, and a router that is overloaded can fail, which overloads its neighbours. This RFC makes a router hold back a route that keeps changing, while leaving stable routes alone.

sections.title: Two Ways to Limit Route Advertisement
sections.content:
The RFC describes two methods of controlling the frequency of route advertisement, and says it is possible and desirable to combine both.

The first uses fixed timers. It has no space overhead per route, but it has the disadvantage of slowing route convergence for the normal case of a route that has no history of instability. The second method overcomes that limitation at the cost of some additional space overhead: a small amount of state per route and a very small processing overhead.

In practice, fixed timers have been set to very short time intervals, and they have proved useful to pack routes into a smaller number of updates when routes arrive in separate updates. The BGP protocol refers to this as packing Network Layer Reachability Information (NLRI). Seldom are fixed timers set to the tens of minutes or hours that would be necessary to actually damp route flap, because doing so would severely limit routing convergence.

For reference, the RFC points at BGP-4, which keeps a Frequency of Route Advertisement section and adds a Frequency of Route Origination section. BGP-4 describes a method involving a fixed, configurable MinRouteAdvertisementInterval timer and a fixed MinASOriginationInterval timer, with recommended values of 30 seconds and 15 seconds. BGP-3, by comparison, makes no specific recommendation in this area.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two ways to slow down route advertisements. Fixed timers hold every route back for the same time, which is simple but delays routes that never misbehave. Damping keeps a small record for each route and holds back only the routes that have a history of changing.

sections.title: What a Damping Algorithm Has to Achieve
sections.content:
The overall objective is to reduce the route update load without limiting convergence time for well behaved routes. To do that, criteria must be defined for well behaved and poorly behaved routes, and the measure used to tell them apart should ideally be a prediction of the future stability of a route.

Several properties follow. Any delay in propagating a well behaved route should be minimal. Delay for a poorly behaved route should, if possible, be proportional to a measure of the expected future instability of the route, and should suppress the unstable route until there is some degree of confidence that it has stabilised. Where routes are unstable, use and announcement of the routes should be suppressed rather than their removal. Where one route to a destination is stable and another is somewhat unstable, the unstable route should be suppressed more aggressively than if there were no alternate path.

Routing consistency matters too. Only very minimal delay should be applied to internal BGP, and it is more desirable to suppress the acceptance of a route, and therefore its use in the IGP, than to suppress only the redistribution. Changes that arrive in separate updates over a very short period, and that could be combined into one update, should be packed as efficiently as possible.

Because nobody can predict the future stability of a route, the recent history of stability is used as the basis for the measure. Two properties of that measure are wanted: the further in the past an instability occurred, the less it should affect the measure, and the measure should be cumulative rather than reflecting only the most recent event. A route with a history of stability that makes a few transitions should make them quickly; if the transitions continue, advertisement of the route should be suppressed, and the memory of prior instability should fade gradually while the route stays announced and stable.
sections.plainLanguage: A damping algorithm has to slow down only the routes that misbehave. It must leave stable routes alone, hold an unstable route back until the route looks settled, and let a route be used again as soon as it has been stable for long enough. It must also keep routing decisions consistent inside one network.

sections.title: Configuration Parameters
sections.content:
The parameters are expressed in units that mean something to the operator, and the run time values are derived from them.

  • The cutoff threshold (cut) is a number of route withdrawals. Above this value a route advertisement is suppressed.
  • The reuse threshold (reuse) is a number of route withdrawals. Below this value a suppressed route is used again.
  • The maximum hold down time (T-hold) is the longest time a route can stay suppressed, however unstable it has been before.
  • The decay half life while reachable (decay-ok) is the time in minutes or seconds in which the accumulated stability figure of merit is halved when the route is considered reachable, whether suppressed or not.
  • The decay half life while unreachable (decay-ng) is the same measure for a route that is considered unreachable. If it is not specified or set to zero, no decay occurs while a route remains unreachable. Decaying at a slower rate than for reachable routes is recommended.
  • The decay memory limit (Tmax-ok or Tmax-ng) is the longest time any memory of previous instability is retained while the route's state stays unchanged. It is generally used to determine array sizes.

A second group applies system wide: the time granularity in seconds used for all decay computations (delta-t), the interval between evaluations of the reuse lists (delta-reuse), the reuse list memory (reuse-list-max), the number of reuse lists (reuse-list-size) and the size of the reuse index array (reuse-index-array-size).

The RFC also allows several sets of these parameters at once. Separate sets can handle short term severe flap and chronic milder flap, which needs a fast decay and a low threshold at one end and a very slow decay and a higher threshold at the other. Different thresholds can be applied to routes with equivalent alternate paths and to routes whose alternate paths have lower bandwidth or tend to be congested. Parameter selection can be based on BGP LOCAL_PREF, on whether an alternate route is known, or on prefix length: longer prefixes tend to reach fewer end systems, are less important, and can be damped more aggressively.
sections.plainLanguage: The operator sets a limit for when to stop advertising a route, a lower limit for when to start again, and how quickly the penalty for a changing route fades. The decay half life is the time it takes for the penalty to halve. Slower decay keeps the memory of a bad period for longer.

sections.title: How the Figure of Merit Changes
sections.content:
The stability figure of merit is an accumulated, time-decayed total. It is increased by 1 each time a route transitions from reachable to unreachable, and it is decayed at a rate proportional to its current value. Because the penalty grows faster the more often a route flaps, a constant flap rate produces a sawtooth: an abrupt rising edge at each flap and a decaying falling edge between flaps. At a continuous constant flap rate the baseline of the sawtooth converges instead of rising forever, unless a ceiling value clips it.

The RFC works one example through. If a route flaps at four times the decay rate, the figure of merit becomes 1, then 1.84, 2.55, 3.14, 3.64, 4.06, 4.42, 4.71, 4.96, 5.17, and so on, converging at about 6.285. Such a route reaches 3 in four cycles, 4 in six cycles and 5 in ten cycles. At twice the decay rate it reaches 3 in seven cycles and converges at a value of less than 3.5.

Figure 1 in the RFC plots the figure of merit for flap at a constant rate, with the time axis in multiples of the decay half life. A ceiling of 4.5 is set, with cutoff and reuse thresholds of 1.5 and 0.75, so that routes are suppressed after being declared unreachable two or three times and used again after approximately two decay half life periods of stability.

The decay is expressed formally. Reachability is a variable R with the value 0 for unreachable and 1 for reachable. At each discrete time the figure of merit is increased by 1 on a transition from R=1 to R=0, and clipped to a ceiling value. Between two discrete times it decays as figure-of-merit(t) = K * figure-of-merit(t - delta-t), where K is K1 for R=0 and K2 for R=1.

The ceiling follows from the other parameters as ceiling = reuse * (exp(T-hold/decay-half-life) * log(2)). The decay applied in one time step is the Nth root of one half, where N is the half life divided by the time granularity. Because exponential decay over a long period can be computed in a single operation regardless of the current value, the decay values can be precomputed into an array at startup and used as a lookup, with an array bound check, a lookup and a multiply.
sections.plainLanguage: Every time a route is withdrawn, one penalty point is added to it. The penalty then fades, faster for a route that is up and more slowly for one that is down. A route that flaps at a steady rate ends up with a penalty that rises and falls around a fixed level instead of growing without limit.

sections.title: Processing Route Updates and Timer Events
sections.content:
The RFC lists the five events an implementation has to handle: a BGP peer or new route comes up for the first time, a route becomes unreachable, a route becomes reachable again, a route changes, and a peer goes down.

When a route becomes unreachable and there is no previous stability history, a damping structure is allocated, the figure of merit is set to 1 and the route is withdrawn. When a history exists, the figure of merit is first decayed over the time since the last update, then 1 is added, and the result is clipped to the ceiling. The route is withdrawn unless it is already suppressed, and it is inserted into a reuse list. A route that becomes reachable again is used immediately if it is not suppressed and its figure of merit is below the cutoff. A suppressed route is used again when the figure of merit falls below the reuse threshold. Otherwise it stays suppressed and is placed on a reuse list. When the figure of merit reaches zero, the memory for the damping structure is recovered.

A route that is replaced by a peer supplying a new path is treated as if an unreachable had been received, and then as an advertisement. The RFC explains why: there is no way to tell whether one of two alternating AS paths is the stable one, so the only viable option is to penalize both routes.

Suppressed routes are held in reuse lists, a circular array of list heads, each list holding routes that are scheduled for reevaluation at about the same time. A reuse index array maps the current figure of merit to the right list, so that choosing a list costs a multiply and shift, a truncation and an array lookup, with no logarithm. Every reuse list interval, the first list is processed and the array is rotated: each route in it is decayed, then either used, disposed of, or placed in another list.

When a peer routing session breaks, the RFC offers two choices: mark each route the peer advertised as unstable, or mark the peering session itself as unstable. Marking the peer saves considerable memory, because routers beyond the immediately adjacent router receive no further advertisements and dispose of the damping structure over time.
sections.plainLanguage: The router reacts to five events: a peer comes up, a route goes down, a route comes back, a route changes and a peer dies. For each route it keeps a penalty. A route with a penalty above the limit is held back and put on a timed list; when the timer reaches it again the penalty is reduced, and the route is used if it has fallen low enough.

sections.title: Deployment Lessons
sections.content:
The RFC reports that the first implementations were the route server daemon (rsd) written by Ramesh Govindan at ISI and the Cisco IOS implementation by Ravi Chandra, both first available in 1995 and used extensively. The rsd implementation was used in route servers at the NSF funded Network Access Points and at other major Internet interconnects, and was integrated into releases of gated. The Cisco IOS version was used by Internet service providers worldwide. At the time of writing there was more than two years of deployment experience.

Two problems had occurred. The first is a configuration mistake with a serious consequence: route damping should never be applied on routes learned from internal BGP, because suppressing them creates inconsistencies inside an AS and route loops can easily form. Implementations should disallow configuration of route damping on internal BGP peers. Penalties should also be applied only when a route is removed or replaced, not when a route is added.

The second is that flapping of a primary path can result in suppression of a secondary path, when no damping is done near the cause of the flap or when a distant AS applies more aggressive damping. The RFC gives two ways out: damp near the source of the flap and make the parameters consistent, or let a distant AS disable penalizing routes on AS path change and penalize only routes that are withdrawn completely.

The RFC also says where damping belongs: near the source of the route flap. Single homed destinations can be covered by static routes, and aggregation provides another means of damping. Providers should damp their own internal problems, damp between their own ASes when they use several, and damp adjacent providers' ASes. Damping state left behind by a fault that has been fixed can be cleared by hand, and providers should publish their damping parameters so that others can tell where damping may have occurred.
sections.plainLanguage: After more than two years of deployment experience, the RFC found that damping works but must be configured carefully. It must not be used on routes learned from inside the same network, because that can create routing loops. It works best close to the source of the problem, and it works badly if one network damps far more aggressively than its neighbour.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says the practices it outlines do not further weaken the security of the routing protocols. Denial of service is possible in an already insecure routing environment, but these practices only contribute to the persistence of such attacks and do not affect the methods of prevention or the methods of determining the source.
sections.plainLanguage: Damping does not make routing less secure. An attacker who can already disrupt routing can keep a disruption going for longer, but damping adds no new way to attack the routing system and does not hide who is responsible.

items.title: Cutoff threshold (cut)
items.text: Above this many withdrawals, a route advertisement is suppressed.

items.title: Reuse threshold (reuse)
items.text: Below this many withdrawals, a suppressed route is used again.

items.title: Maximum hold down (T-hold)
items.text: The longest time a route can stay suppressed.

items.title: Decay half life while reachable (decay-ok)
items.text: Time in which the penalty is halved for a reachable route.

items.title: Decay half life while unreachable (decay-ng)
items.text: Time in which the penalty is halved for an unreachable route.

items.title: Decay memory limit (Tmax)
items.text: How long the memory of earlier instability is kept.

viz.caption: RULES THE RFC LEARNS FROM DEPLOYMENT

items.title: Never damp internal routes
items.text: Suppressing routes learned from internal peers can create persistent route loops.

items.title: Damp near the source
items.text: Flapping is best contained close to where it happens.

items.title: Keep parameters consistent
items.text: A distant network damping harder can suppress a good secondary path.

items.title: Publish your parameters
items.text: Others need them to tell where damping may have happened.
